title: Marks on the page
goal: Read the two marks, the letter-numbers and the abbreviations a real page is full of.

sections.body: Hebrew has two punctuation marks of its own, and neither is an apostrophe or a quotation mark, though both are typed with those keys. They mark shortened words, and a printed page is full of them.

what it means
example
rows: ׳ on a letter — a foreign sound

sections.body: The gershayim sits before the last letter of the abbreviation, which is how you tell it from a quotation mark at a glance. And letters do duty as numbers: א is 1, י is 10, ק is 100 — so a page number, a chapter, or a Hebrew year is spelled rather than counted.

sections.caption: Abbreviations you will meet on any page
head: short
meaning
written out

sections.body: An abbreviation you cannot crack is usually a source rather than a word — a title, a tractate, an author — and older printing shortens exactly those the hardest. When one blocks a sentence, read past it: it is almost always a citation you can look up later.

Nothing in a Hebrew text tells you where a quotation begins — quotation marks are recent, and older books use none. In Bialik or Brenner, speech is often marked by nothing but a dash at the start of the line.
